title: Searching a Concatenated Value Blocks the Seek
description: Concatenating columns to compare (first + ' ' + last) can't seek; compare the underlying indexed columns instead. Why it matters: "full name" and other concatenated-field searches are extremely common in application code, and this is exactly why they don't scale without a rewrite.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a subtle non-sargability trap that's specific to text search: comparing a *concatenated* combination of columns — `FirstName + ' ' + LastName = 'John Smith'` — instead of comparing the underlying columns directly. It's an incredibly natural way to write a "search by full name" feature, since users think of "full name" as one thing, not two separate database columns — but it completely disables even a well-designed composite index on `(LastName, FirstName)`.

The mechanism here is, once again, a variation on the same core idea running through this whole course section: an index only helps you seek when the comparison is against the *raw, stored* values it contains, in the order it's sorted by. `FirstName + ' ' + LastName` is not a stored value anywhere — it's a brand-new string, freshly assembled by gluing two column values (plus a literal space) together, computed at query time for each row. There's no index anywhere that has a pre-sorted list of "every row's first name plus a space plus their last name," because that string doesn't exist until the concatenation actually happens. So SQL Server has no choice but to visit every row in the table, build that concatenated string fresh, and then compare it to `'John Smith'` — a full scan, with string-building work added on top for every row, even though there's a perfectly good composite index sitting right there on `(LastName, FirstName)` — a pair of columns this exact search is fundamentally about.

The fix is to recognize that "full name equals X" is really two separate, simple conditions joined together, and to write it that way: split the search term back into its first-name and last-name parts (in application code, before the query even runs), and compare each part to its own raw column — `WHERE LastName = 'Smith' AND FirstName = 'John'`. Written this way, there's no concatenation, no computed expression, nothing standing between the query and the raw, indexed column values. And because there's already a composite index on `(LastName, FirstName)` — matching this exact equality-then-equality pattern — SQL Server can seek directly to the handful of rows where both conditions are true, instead of scanning the whole table.

This connects nicely back to the composite-key-ordering lesson elsewhere in this course: notice that the index is built `(LastName, FirstName)` — last name first — and the rewritten query filters on both as straight equalities, so column order barely matters here compared to the equality-versus-range lesson (both conditions are equality, so either order would let the engine seek reasonably well) — but it's still worth building the index with whichever column is more commonly searched alone as the lead column, in case some future query filters only by last name.

It's worth being honest that this specific fix (splitting a search term into first/last name in application code) requires you to actually know, structurally, what the user typed — "John Smith" needs to be split into "John" and "Smith" by *your application*, which is straightforward for a simple two-part name but gets genuinely harder for messier real-world names (multiple middle names, single-word names, names with punctuation). In cases where you can't cleanly split the search term, other options exist — like full-text search features built specifically for searching across text, or maintaining a separate, always-up-to-date computed column that stores the concatenated full name (kept automatically in sync by the database itself) and indexing *that* — but the simplest, cheapest fix, whenever it's available, is exactly what this lesson shows: stop concatenating at query time, and compare the real underlying columns instead.

Why does this matter broadly? "Search by full name" (or "search by full address," or any other feature that glues several columns together conceptually) is an extremely common UI pattern, and the natural, human way to think about the search — "does the full name match" — maps directly onto the non-sargable, concatenated version of the query if you're not paying attention. Recognizing string concatenation (or any other expression combining multiple columns) inside a `WHERE` clause as a red flag, and instead asking "can I express this as separate conditions against the raw, individual columns," is a pattern worth having ready any time you're building search features.

It's useful to generalize this beyond "full name" specifically: any time a query combines two or more columns together with `+` (or `CONCAT()`) before comparing the combined result to something, you've created the same non-sargable shape — "full address" built from street, city, and zip; a "display code" built from a prefix plus an ID; a computed label built from several fields. In every one of these cases, the fix follows the same pattern shown in this lesson: figure out what the combined value is actually testing for, and see if that same real-world condition can instead be expressed as separate comparisons against each underlying raw column. This isn't always possible cleanly (sometimes the combined value genuinely doesn't map back to simple per-column conditions, especially with fuzzy or partial text matching), but it's worth checking first, because when it works, it's by far the cheapest fix available — no new indexes, no schema changes, just restructuring how the search condition is expressed to match how the data is actually stored and sorted.

One more thing worth knowing: SQL Server's optimizer has gotten smarter over the years about certain limited concatenation patterns, but you should never assume this without checking -- the safest default assumption is that any expression combining multiple columns inside a WHERE clause will not be sargable, and the burden is on you to verify otherwise by actually inspecting the execution plan rather than hoping for the best.

As a final practical note, this same principle -- prefer comparing raw underlying columns over comparing a computed combination of them -- extends well beyond string concatenation. Any derived value assembled from several columns at query time, whether through string-building, arithmetic, or conditional logic, tends to break index seeks in exactly the same way, for exactly the same underlying reason: the index has no pre-built, sorted copy of a value that only comes into existence when the query runs.

## Scenario
A "search by full name" feature runs `WHERE FirstName + ' ' + LastName = 'John Smith'` against a 200,000-row `Customers` table that already has a composite index on `(LastName, FirstName)`. The index is never used.

## Why it's slow
`FirstName + ' ' + LastName` is an **expression computed from the columns** — the engine can't know which index entry equals `'John Smith'` without first building the concatenation for **every** row. That makes the predicate **non-sargable**, so SQL Server falls back to a full **Index Scan** and evaluates the concatenation as a residual filter.

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** (not a Seek) on `Customers`, reading all 200k rows.
- The concatenation appearing as a Compute Scalar / residual predicate rather than a seek predicate.

## The concept
Anything that wraps the indexed columns — a function, arithmetic, or a **concatenation** — hides the raw values the index is sorted on. Compare the columns **individually** (`FirstName = 'John' AND LastName = 'Smith'`) and the composite index seeks straight to the rows. Same result, a scan of 200k rows becomes a handful of reads.
hints: The predicate compares a concatenation, not the columns themselves — the index can't seek on a value it must compute per row.
Split the search into the underlying columns so each can be matched against the index key.
Use WHERE FirstName = 'John' AND LastName = 'Smith'; — the (LastName, FirstName) index now seeks.
